routes.label: Identify each maa by its two pibs

question:
Given a set \(S\) consisting of two undefined elements “pib” and “maa,” and the four postulates:

\(\mathrm{P}_1:\) Every pib is a collection of maas.

\(\mathrm{P}_2:\) Any two distinct pibs have one and only one maa in common.

\(\mathrm{P}_3:\) Every maa belongs to two and only two pibs.

\(\mathrm{P}_4:\) There are exactly four pibs.

Consider the three theorems:

\(\mathrm{T}_1:\) There are exactly six maas.

\(\mathrm{T}_2:\) There are exactly three maas in each pib.

\(\mathrm{T}_3:\) For each maa there is exactly one other maa not in the same pib with it.

The theorems which are deducible from the postulates are:
solution:
Label the four pibs \(A,B,C,D\). By \(\mathrm{P}_2\), every pair of distinct pibs has exactly one common maa. By \(\mathrm{P}_3\), that maa belongs to exactly those two pibs.

Different pairs must give different maas: a maa serving two different pairs would belong to at least three pibs, contradicting \(\mathrm{P}_3\). Conversely, every maa belongs to exactly two pibs, so it comes from one of these pairs. Thus the maas correspond exactly to
\[
AB,\ AC,\ AD,\ BC,\ BD,\ CD.
\]
There are six pairs, proving \(\mathrm{T}_1\), with neither omitted nor repeated maas.

The maas in pib \(A\) are precisely those represented by \(AB,AC,AD\), so \(A\) contains three maas. The same argument applies to each of the four pibs, proving \(\mathrm{T}_2\).

Finally, take any maa and call its two pibs \(A,B\). Another maa shares no pib with it exactly when its pair uses neither \(A\) nor \(B\). The only such pair is \(CD\), and it represents exactly one maa. This proves \(\mathrm{T}_3\).

All three theorems follow, so the answer is \(\boxed{\mathrm{E}}\).
